issues.explanation: Checking surroundings implies an active current-threat/hypervigilance pattern, but the formulation has Threat disconnected from all other active nodes and Triggers also inactive. With no Threat items present and no active links involving Threat or Triggers, this strategy is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life not worth living anymore' suggests a marked hopeless/depressive or self-destructive appraisal. The rest of the selected items center on fragmented trauma memory and avoidance/social distraction, without other items indicating pervasive defeat, guilt, permanent damage, or a threat-related meaning that would make this severe appraisal cohere strongly.

vignette:
The accident happened on a rain-slicked highway outside Austin, during the final leg of a regional tour. Marco, a thirty-five-year-old musician, had been in the passenger seat of the van when a semi-truck drifted into their lane. He remembers the screech of metal, the violent spin, and then nothing. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened next, the memory becomes a wall of static. He can only retrieve fragmented pieces—the smell of diesel, the sight of his own hand, bloodied, resting on the shattered glass, and a paramedic’s face asking him questions he could not answer. The memory feels incomplete, like a film reel with most of the frames cut out, and this gap has become its own source of torment. He is certain that the missing pieces hold something terrible, something he cannot bear to know, and that this is just one more way the trauma has stolen from him. Because the memory feels broken, Marco has come to believe that his life is fundamentally destroyed—that the person he was before the crash is gone, and that all that remains is a shattered, angry version of himself.

In the months since, Marco has developed a desperate strategy to avoid being alone. He keeps himself constantly surrounded by people, filling every evening with jam sessions, bar gigs, or late-night hangs at friends’ apartments. He has become the person who always says yes to an invitation, because the moment the door closes and the silence settles, the fragmented images surface, and he is back in that spinning van. This constant socialising is driven by a deep fear: he is convinced that if he ever sits still long enough to think, the rage he feels about the accident—about the driver who was never charged, about the injustice of it all—will consume him. He is terrified that he will not be able to control his anger and will do something terrible, so he keeps the noise of other people around him as a dam against that flood. When he does talk, he avoids any mention of the crash or its aftermath, steering conversations toward music or sports or anything else. But the socialising itself has created a paradox: the more he talks and laughs with others, the more exhausted he becomes, and the more his mind wanders into those disconnected pieces, making the memory even harder to piece together. He has noticed that after a long night of performing, he wakes with even less clarity about the event, as if the effort of avoidance has further scrambled the fragments.

Marco’s wife, Elena, has watched him change. He used to be the one who would sit on the porch and write lyrics for hours, but now he cannot bear the quiet. She has tried to get him to talk about the accident, but he shuts down immediately. He has stopped going to the studio alone, insisting that a bandmate or producer be present whenever he records. His career, once on an upward trajectory, has stalled—he turned down a solo residency because it would have meant spending long nights alone in a hotel room. He tells himself that his life has been destroyed by the trauma, and that this is just the new reality. The injustice of it all gnaws at him daily: the truck driver faced no consequences, while Marco’s sense of self and safety have been erased. He is certain that if he ever lets himself fully feel that rage, he will lose control and hurt someone, so he keeps smiling, keeps playing, keeps the crowd around him. But last week, after a gig, he found himself alone in the parking lot for thirty seconds before a friend came out, and in that brief moment he saw the paramedic’s face again, and his hands began to shake. That was the moment he finally agreed to call a therapist. What frightens him most is not the memory itself, but the fear of what he might become if he ever stops running from it.
